newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Trade partners press U.S. to back telecom pact.
newsitem.headline: Trade partners press U.S. to back telecom pact.

text.p: Major trading powers piled pressure on the United States on Friday to agree to what they said was a potentially powerful pact to open up the booming telecommunications industry to worldwide competition.

U.S. officials close to the World Trade Organisation talks in Geneva, while declining to comment on prospects for an accord, indicated that a decision was in the works in Washington and could be announced later.
The negotiations faced a deadline of midnight in Geneva (6 p.m. EST).

A senior negotiator from Canada, which has been strongly targeted by Washington for offering to allow only 46.7 percent foreign ownership of its domestic telecommunications companies, said he could not believe the United States would walk away from a deal now.
Such action, he said, would ignore "economic and commercial good sense," adding: "I think that at the end of the day, rationality will prevail and we will all sign."
European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan suggested the United States would be "crazy" not to go along with the pact.
"What is on the table amounts to a massive liberalisation of the world telecommunication market that it would be crazy not to grab with both hands," Brittan told a news conference.
"I see no conceivable justification on the basis of what is on the table for failing to clinch the deal."

The long-negotiated pact is billed by WTO analysts as holding the prospect of bringing telephone charges for ordinary users and business tumbling around the globe and boosting markets for new equipment and services.

In a report issued Friday, the International Telecommunications Union predicted that global revenues for the industry would jump from $800 billion last year to $1.2 trillion at the turn of the century if the deal goes through.
The United States, however, is vital for a meaningful pact since it is the world's largest single telecommunications market, accounting for just under a third of the annual total.

Last April Washington sunk an earlier bid to get a pact when it walked away from talks just before a previous deadline saying offers from other countries, primarily emerging economies, were not good enough.
U.S. officials say that to ensure strong public and Congressional backing for a deal at home, it has to be clearly "equitable" with wide enough openings from other countries to match their own offer.

Throughout this week the U.S. officials insisted that improvements in openings currently on the table were needed to finalise a pact. The United States package proposes a full opening of its domestic market to all comers.

Britain, sometimes more attuned to U.S. thinking on economic matters than it is to that of its EU partners, joined the chorus of appeals to Washington to line up behind the deal, which would link a total of 61 countries.

"I would certainly urge the Americans to live up to their rhetoric .... and sign up to an accord," Minister for Science and Technology Ian Taylor told another Geneva news conference as the word from Washington was anxiously awaited.

Japanese officials have also said the market opening offers now on the table, which include many from emerging economies who did not join the last round of talks, appeared to be a good deal and should be sealed in a pact.
